an4.159:1.2: that on one occasion Ven. Ānanda was staying in Kosambī at Ghosita’s monastery.
an4.159:1.3: Then a certain nun said to a certain man,
an4.159:1.4: “Go, my good man, to my lord Ānanda and, on arrival, bowing your head to his feet in my name, tell him,
an4.159:1.5: ‘The nun named such-&-such, venerable sir, is sick, in pain, severely ill.
an4.159:1.6: She bows her head to the feet of her lord Ānanda and says,
an4.159:1.7: “It would be good if my lord Ānanda were to go to the nuns’ quarters, to visit this nun out of sympathy for her.”’”
an4.159:1.8: Responding, “Yes, my lady,” the man then went to Ven. Ānanda and, on arrival, having bowed down, sat to one side. As he was sitting there he said to Ven. Ānanda,
an4.159:2.1: “The nun named such-&-such, venerable sir, is sick, in pain, severely ill.
an4.159:2.2: She bows her head to the feet of her lord Ānanda and says,
an4.159:2.3: ‘It would be good if my lord Ānanda were to go to the nuns’ quarters, to visit this nun out of sympathy for her.’”
an4.159:3.1: Then in the early morning, having adjusted his lower robe and carrying his bowl & outer robe, Ven. Ānanda went to the nuns’ quarters.
an4.159:3.2: The nun saw Ven. Ānanda coming from afar.
an4.159:3.3: On seeing him, she lay down on a bed, having covered her head.
an4.159:3.4: Then Ven. Ānanda went to the nun and, on arrival, sat down on a seat made ready. As he was sitting there, he said to the nun:
an4.159:4.1: “This body, sister, comes into being through food.
an4.159:4.2: And yet it is by relying on food that food is to be abandoned.
an4.159:4.3: “This body comes into being through craving.
an4.159:4.4: And yet it is by relying on craving that craving is to be abandoned.
an4.159:4.5: “This body comes into being through conceit.
an4.159:4.6: And yet it is by relying on conceit that conceit is to be abandoned.
an4.159:4.7: “This body comes into being through sexual intercourse. Sexual intercourse is to be abandoned.
an4.159:4.8: With regard to sexual intercourse, the Buddha declares the cutting-off of the bridge.
an4.159:5.1: “‘This body, sister, comes into being through food.
an4.159:5.2: And yet it is by relying on food that food is to be abandoned.’ Thus it was said.
an4.159:5.3: And in reference to what was it said?
an4.159:5.4: There is the case, sister, where a monk, considering it thoughtfully, takes food—
an4.159:5.5: not playfully, nor for intoxication, nor for putting on bulk, nor for beautification—but simply for the survival & continuance of this body, for ending its afflictions, for the support of the holy life, (thinking,) ‘Thus will I destroy old feelings (of hunger) and not create new feelings (from overeating). I will maintain myself, be blameless, & live in comfort.’
an4.159:5.6: Then, at a later time, he abandons food, having relied on food.
an4.159:5.7: ‘This body, sister, comes into being through food. And yet it is by relying on food that food is to be abandoned.’ Thus it was said.
an4.159:5.8: And in reference to this was it said.
an4.159:6.1: “‘This body comes into being through craving.
an4.159:6.2: And yet it is by relying on craving that craving is to be abandoned.’ Thus it was said.
an4.159:6.3: And in reference to what was it said?
an4.159:6.4: There is the case, sister, where a monk hears,
an4.159:6.5: ‘The monk named such-&-such, they say, through the ending of the effluents, has entered & remains in the effluent-free awareness-release & discernment-release, having known & realized them for himself right in the here & now.’
an4.159:6.7: ‘I hope that I, too, will—through the ending of the effluents—enter & remain in the effluent-free awareness-release & discernment-release, having directly known & realized them for myself right in the here & now.’
an4.159:6.8: Then, at a later time, he abandons craving, having relied on craving.
an4.159:6.9: ‘This body comes into being through craving.
an4.159:6.10: And yet it is by relying on craving that craving is to be abandoned.’ Thus it was said.
an4.159:7.1: And in reference to this was it said.
an4.159:7.2: “‘This body comes into being through conceit. And yet it is by relying on conceit that conceit is to be abandoned.’ Thus it was said.
an4.159:7.3: And in reference to what was it said?
an4.159:7.4: There is the case, sister, where a monk hears,
an4.159:7.5: ‘The monk named such-&-such, they say, through the ending of the effluents, has entered & remains in the effluent-free awareness-release & discernment-release, having directly known & realized them for himself right in the here & now.’
an4.159:7.7: ‘The monk named such-&-such, they say, through the ending of the effluents, has entered & remains in the effluent-free awareness-release & discernment-release, having directly known & realized them for himself right in the here & now.
an4.159:7.9: Then, at a later time, he abandons conceit, having relied on conceit.
an4.159:7.10: ‘This body comes into being through conceit. And yet it is by relying on conceit that conceit is to be abandoned.’ Thus it was said.
an4.159:7.11: And in reference to this was it said.
an4.159:8.1: “This body comes into being through sexual intercourse. Sexual intercourse is to be abandoned.
an4.159:8.2: With regard to sexual intercourse, the Buddha declares the cutting-off of the bridge.”
an4.159:9.1: Then the nun—getting up from her bed, arranging her upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing down with her head at Ven. Ānanda’s feet—said,
an4.159:9.2: “A transgression has overcome me, venerable sir, in that I was so foolish, so muddle-headed, and so unskilled as to act in this way.
an4.159:9.3: May my lord Ānanda please accept this confession of my transgression as such, so that I may restrain myself in the future.”
an4.159:9.4: “Yes, sister, a transgression overcame you in that you were so foolish, so muddle-headed, and so unskilled as to act in this way.
an4.159:9.5: But because you see your transgression as such and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept your confession.
an4.159:9.6: For it is a cause of growth in the discipline of the noble ones when, seeing a transgression as such, one makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma and exercises restraint in the future.”
